notes.meaning: God gave Moses instructions to set apart Aaron and his sons to serve as priests. To begin, Moses had to take one young bull and two rams that had no flaws or injuries. Sacrificing animals without defects showed that God deserves the very best, pointing ahead to the pure and sinless life of Jesus.

Moses was told to gather three kinds of bread made from fine wheat flour and olive oil, without any yeast. These loaves, cakes, and thin wafers were placed into a single basket to be presented at the sacred tent alongside the animals. Because yeast often represented decay or sin, unleavened bread symbolized purity and true sincerity before God.

Moses brought Aaron and his sons to the entrance of the Tent of Meeting to wash them completely with water. This public washing showed that no one can come near a holy God while stained by the dirt of sin. It was an outward sign of spiritual cleansing before they put on their holy priestly clothes.

Moses dressed Aaron in the sacred high-priestly garments, starting with the inner linen tunic and moving outward. He placed on him the blue robe, the colorful vest called the ephod, the chestpiece, and the special waistband. Dressing Aaron in these holy clothes showed everyone that he was being officially placed into his sacred office.

Moses placed a linen turban on Aaron's head and attached the holy gold diadem to the front of it. This golden plate had the words 'Holiness to the LORD' carved into it like a royal crown. It gave the high priest great dignity and reminded the people that he was devoted completely to God.

Moses took the specially perfumed anointing oil and poured it directly over Aaron's head. Pouring the oil generously showed that God was pouring out the Holy Spirit to prepare and empower Aaron for his duties. This special ceremony pointed forward to Jesus, whose title Christ means 'the Anointed One.'

Moses brought Aaron's sons forward, dressed them in linen tunics, wrapped sashes around them, and tied headbands on their heads. God declared that the priesthood would belong to Aaron and his family line by a lasting rule through every generation. In this way, Moses ordained them by placing their holy work directly into their hands.

Moses brought the young bull to the front of the tent, and Aaron and his sons pressed their hands firmly on its head. This action showed that they were identifying with the animal and admitting their own guilt before God. By placing their hands there, they asked God to accept the animal's life in place of their own.

Moses slaughtered the bull in the presence of the Lord at the entrance of the Tent of Meeting. Because Aaron and his sons were not yet fully ordained priests, Moses performed the sacrifice for them. This sacrifice was carried out publicly before God to begin their cleansing.

Moses dipped his finger into the bull's blood and smeared it onto the four raised corners, or horns, of the altar. Afterward, he poured out the rest of the blood at the base of the altar. Putting blood on the altar cleansed and set apart the altar itself, making it ready for holy worship.

Moses took the fat covering the internal organs, the lobe of the liver, and both kidneys with their fat, burning them on the altar fire. In ancient times, the rich inner fat was considered the best and most valuable part of the animal. Burning it gave the richest portion directly to God as a gift of honor.

Moses carried the rest of the bull—its meat, hide, and waste—outside the camp and burned it all completely with fire. Because this was a sin offering to remove guilt, none of its meat could be eaten or kept within the community. It showed how completely sin must be taken away from the camp where God lived with His people.

Moses brought out the first ram, and Aaron and his sons laid their hands upon its head. This animal was chosen to be a burnt offering rather than a sin offering. By placing their hands on the ram, the priests offered themselves completely to God alongside the sacrifice.

Moses slaughtered the ram and splashed its blood against all sides of the altar. Throwing the blood around the altar marked the entire altar with the life of the sacrifice. It showed that God's people can only come near to Him through the cleansing power of sacrificial blood.

Moses cut the ram into pieces, washed its legs and inner parts with water, and placed the whole animal on the altar. He burned the entire ram so that the smoke rose up as a burnt offering to the Lord. The sacrifice was called a pleasing aroma because God gladly accepted their sincere devotion and complete dedication.

Moses brought the second ram, which was called the ram of ordination, and Aaron and his sons placed their hands on its head. This special animal served like a fellowship offering that sealed the sacred relationship between God and the new priests. It formed the central step in setting them apart for their holy work.

Moses slaughtered the ram and touched some of its blood to the right earlobes, right thumbs, and right big toes of Aaron and his sons. The ear meant listening closely to God's word, the hand meant doing His work, and the foot meant walking in His ways. Placing blood on these parts dedicated their whole bodies and daily lives entirely to God's service.

Moses took blood from the altar together with the holy anointing oil and sprinkled it on Aaron, his sons, and their priestly clothes. This combined sprinkling of blood and oil set them and their garments apart as completely holy to the Lord. It pictured the need for both forgiveness through sacrifice and spiritual renewal through the Holy Spirit.

Moses gathered the rich fat portions of the ordination ram, including the broad fat tail, the kidney fat, and the right thigh, along with three kinds of unleavened bread from the basket. The wide tail of eastern sheep was prized as the finest delicacy, while the bread formed a grain gift of thanksgiving. All these choice items were gathered so they could be placed into the priests' hands to complete their ordination.
